warmup.q: A sort-merge join of 1,000,000 payments with 500 merchants runs in 16 reduce tasks. One merchant has 30% of the payments. The 15 other tasks take about 40 ms each. About how long does the join stage take?
options: About 40 ms, because the tasks run in parallel
About 16 x 40 = 640 ms, because the tasks run one after another
About 8 times 40 ms: as long as the one task that got the big merchant
About 40 ms, because Spark spreads the big merchant's rows over all 16 tasks
warmup.why: Hash partitioning sends every row of one key to one task, so the task that owns the big merchant fetches about 346,000 records while the median task fetches about 43,000: 8 times as many. A stage ends when its last task ends. Spark doesn't spread a key over tasks by itself; that's what AQE's skew handling and salting are for, and the skew demo measures all of it.

sections.h: Catalyst rewrites your query as a tree, one rule at a time
sections.html:
Lesson 6 (The Spark execution model) showed that explain("extended") prints four plans. The Storage track's lesson on query optimization showed a single-machine optimizer rewriting a plan with rules and choosing joins from cardinality estimates. Spark's optimizer does the same for a cluster, then corrects its estimates while the job runs. This lesson opens up both, and then two problems no optimizer fixes on its own: one hot key, and results you compute twice. Take a question from the fraud team: Dutch card payments over 1,000 euros at merchants with category code 5001.

SELECT m.merchant_name, p.amount_cents
FROM payments p JOIN merchants m ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id
WHERE p.card_country = 'NL' AND m.mcc = 5001 AND p.amount_cents > 100 * 1000

Read literally, this says: join every payment to its merchant, then keep the rows that match. Version 1 runs it that way. The join handles all 1,000,000 payments and all six of their columns, and the filter then throws away about 996 rows in every 1,000: one card in 8 is Dutch, one merchant in 20 has code 5001, and 60% of amounts are above 100,000 cents. A person would filter each table first and carry only the three columns the answer needs. Version 2 is a program that makes those edits for every query, mechanically.

That program is Catalyst, Spark SQL's optimizer. It holds a query as a tree of operators: here a Filter node with a Join node under it, and a table at each leaf. A rule is a function from a tree to a tree that looks for one pattern and rewrites it. PushDownPredicates looks for a filter sitting above a join, splits its condition at each AND, and moves each part down to the side whose columns it uses. ColumnPruning removes columns that nothing above uses. ConstantFolding turns 100 * 1000 into 100000 once, instead of once per row. Catalyst groups rules into batches and runs each batch again and again until a pass changes nothing, a fixed point.

The four plans are the four steps of that work:

  1. Parsed: the tree as written. Names carry a quote mark, 'UnresolvedRelation [payments], because nothing has been looked up yet.
  2. Analyzed: names resolved against the catalog. payments becomes a Parquet relation with six typed columns, and a misspelled column fails here, before any job runs.
  3. Optimized: rules applied. The filter is split three ways: card_country = 'NL' and amount_cents > 100000 go down the payments side, mcc = 5001 down the merchants side. InferFiltersFromConstraints added isnotnull(merchant_id), because an inner join can never match a null key, so those rows can go early.
  4. Physical: each logical node becomes an operator that can run. Merchants are small, so the join becomes a broadcast hash join (lesson 7), and the scan gets PushedFilters and a three-column ReadSchema (lesson 5).

When the plan runs, operators in the same stage are fused by whole-stage code generation: the *(1) in front of them means Spark wrote one Java method for the whole chain, so a row doesn't pass through a virtual call per operator.

In the Try it, Spark tried 100 optimizer rules on this query, and 6 changed it. Catalyst has two blind spots. It can't see inside your code: a Kotlin lambda or a UDF is opaque, so no filter is pushed through it (lesson 9 shows this). And every physical choice in step 4 rests on size estimates. The next section is about what happens when they're wrong.

try.title: Watch the filter move
steps: From the labs folder, run OptimizerDemo. It registers a million payments and 500 merchants as views, plans the fraud team's query and prints the four plans without running anything.
Before reading: in the optimized plan, which side of the join will mcc = 5001 be on, and what will 100 * 1000 have become?
Compare the Filter in the analyzed plan with the ones in the optimized plan. Which rule in the list at the end did each change?

code.title: OptimizerDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l08.demo import scala.jdk.javaapi.CollectionConverters /** * One SQL query through Catalyst's four plans, and the optimizer rules that changed it. Nothing * runs: explain() only plans. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() demoPayments(spark).createOrReplaceTempView("payments") demoMerchants(spark).createOrReplaceTempView("merchants") val df = spark.sql( """ SELECT m.merchant_name, p.amount_cents FROM payments p JOIN merchants m ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id WHERE p.card_country = 'NL' AND m.mcc = 5001 AND p.amount_cents > 100 * 1000 """.trimIndent() ) val qe = df.queryExecution() println("== 1. parsed: your words, nothing looked up yet ==") println(clean(qe.logical())) println("== 2. analyzed: names resolved against the catalog ==") println(clean(qe.analyzed())) println("== 3. optimized: rewritten by rules ==") println(clean(qe.optimizedPlan())) println("== 4. physical: the operators that will run ==") println(clean(qe.executedPlan())) val prefix = "org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.optimizer." val fired = CollectionConverters.asJava(qe.tracker().rules()) .filter { (name, s) -> name.startsWith(prefix) && s.numEffectiveInvocations() > 0 } .keys.map { it.removePrefix(prefix) }.sorted() val tried = CollectionConverters.asJava(qe.tracker().rules()).keys.count { it.startsWith(prefix) } println("optimizer rules tried: $tried, rules that changed the plan: ${fired.size}") fired.forEach { println(" $it") } spark.stop() }

(physical plan trimmed)
optimizer rules tried: 100, rules that changed the plan: 6

The parsed plan has the whole Filter above the Join, with quoted, unresolved names. In the optimized plan the filter is gone from the top: the payments side has card_country = NL and amount_cents > 100000 (the 100 * 1000 was folded), plus isnotnull checks that InferFiltersFromConstraints added, and the merchants side has the mcc test, pushed all the way down to the Range that generates the merchants. A Project [merchant_id, amount_cents] now sits on the payments side: ColumnPruning dropped the other four, and the physical scan reads three: those two plus card_country, which the filter needs. Optimizer$FinishAnalysis cleaned up what analysis left behind, such as the SubqueryAlias and View wrappers.

sections.h: AQE plans again at every shuffle, with real sizes
sections.html:
Catalyst plans before a single row is read, so it plans from estimates. For a file, the estimate is its size on disk. After a filter, Spark usually can't tell how many rows survive (unless someone collected column statistics, which few pipelines do), so it keeps the input's estimate.

The Try it shows how far off that can be. It joins a million payments with the payments over 2,499 euros, on card_id, to find other payments made with cards that made a very large one. The planner estimates the flagged side at 3.9 MiB: the two columns it reads, as if the filter kept every row. It really has 747 rows. Lesson 7's rule is to broadcast a side below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold. The demo's tables are about a thousand times smaller than a real day of payments, so it lowers that threshold from 10 MB to 1 MB. Now 3.9 MiB looks too big, and Spark plans a sort-merge join with a shuffle under each side.

Version 1: plan once and live with it. That's Spark with AQE off: both sides shuffled and sorted, for a table of 747 rows.

Version 2: plan again once you know. The shuffle gives Spark a natural pause. Every map task of a shuffle must finish before any reduce task starts (lesson 7), and when the last one finishes, the driver knows exactly how many bytes went to each reduce partition. Adaptive query execution (AQE), on by default since Spark 3.2, uses that pause. It cuts the physical plan at every Exchange into query stages and runs the stages whose inputs are ready, each as a job of its own. Each time one finishes, AQE optimizes the rest of the plan again, with measured sizes in place of the estimates, and then runs the next stages, until the last one. The stepper below walks through it.

At each pause AQE can change three things. It merges small neighbouring partitions (AQEShuffleRead coalesced, from lesson 7). It switches a sort-merge join to a broadcast hash join when one side turned out smaller than spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, which is the same as the planning threshold unless you set it. And it splits skewed partitions, which is the next section. Spark 4.3 added a fourth, on by default: turning a sort-merge join into a shuffled hash join (lesson 7) when it judges each partition's hash table small enough to build, which saves the sort. The labs' Spark 4.1 only does that if you set spark.sql.adaptive.maxShuffledHashJoinLocalMapThreshold.

How much does all this buy? When AQE arrived in Spark 3.0, still off by default, Databricks reported that on the TPC-DS benchmark it made 32 queries more than 1.1 times faster, the best of them 8 times faster. Nearly all of that came from merging partitions and switching joins, because TPC-DS data has no skew; the skew handling paid off in production workloads instead.

The plan shows all of this. Before the action, explain() prints AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false and the plan from estimates. After it, the final plan, with ShuffleQueryStage and BroadcastQueryStage nodes for the stages that ran. In the Try it, the final plan has a BroadcastHashJoin, and the run took about half as long.

The switch comes late, so it isn't free. Both map stages ran before AQE could compare the two sides, so the million payments were still written to shuffle files: 8.66 MB of shuffle write with AQE on, the same as with it off. AQE then reads those files where they are, with a local shuffle reader (AQEShuffleRead local), so nothing crosses the network and nothing is sorted. Spark's tuning guide puts it plainly: this is better than going on with the sort-merge join, and worse than planning the broadcast from the start. When you know a side is small, lesson 7's broadcast() hint still wins.

code.title: AqeDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l08.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col /** * Joins a million payments with the few flagged ones on card_id. Spark's estimate for the * filtered side is megabytes; the real size is a few kilobytes. With AQE off, Spark keeps the * sort-merge join it planned. With AQE on, it re-plans after the first stages and broadcasts. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() // this laptop table is 14 MB, not 14 GB: shrink the broadcast threshold from 10 MB to 1 MB to match spark.conf().set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "1MB") val log = TaskLog(spark) val payments = demoPayments(spark) val flagged = payments.where(col("amount_cents").gt(249_900)).select(col("card_id"), col("payment_id").alias("flagged_payment")) println("planner's size estimate for the flagged side: ${flagged.queryExecution().optimizedPlan().stats().simpleString()}") println("rows it really has: ${flagged.count()}") for (aqe in listOf(false, true)) { spark.conf().set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", aqe.toString()) fun query() = payments.join(flagged, "card_id").groupBy("card_country").count() query().collectAsList() // warm-up val df = query() val t0 = System.nanoTime() val (jobs, stages) = log.run { df.collectAsList() } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6 println() println("AQE ${if (aqe) "on" else "off"}: %d job(s), tasks per stage %s, shuffle write %,d bytes, %.0f ms" .format(jobs, stages.values.map { it.size }, log.bytesWritten(), ms)) val plan = df.queryExecution().executedPlan() if (aqe) { val text = clean(plan) val final = text.substringAfter("== Final Plan ==").substringBefore("== Initial Plan ==") val initial = text.substringAfter("== Initial Plan ==") println(" initial plan: " + planLines(initial, "Join").joinToString()) println(" final plan:") planLines(final, "Join", "QueryStage", "AQEShuffleRead", "Exchange").forEach { println(" $it") } } else { planLines(plan, "Join", "Exchange").forEach { println(" $it") } } } spark.stop() }

The estimate came from file sizes and the columns read; the filter's real selectivity, 747 rows out of a million, was invisible to the planner. AQE off ran one job with four stages and kept the sort-merge join. AQE on ran five jobs, one per query stage: the two map sides (4 tasks each), the broadcast build (1 task), the join with the partial count (4 tasks) and the final count, coalesced into 1 task. Its initial plan was the same sort-merge join; its final plan has a BroadcastHashJoin fed by a BroadcastQueryStage. The shuffle write is the same 8.66 MB in both runs, because the payments' map stage had already written its files before AQE re-planned. sections.h: One hot key makes one task do the work of many
sections.html:
A marketplace merchant changes the shape of the data. In the Try it, merchant 7 has 30% of a million payments, and the join with the merchants runs as a sort-merge join into 16 partitions. Hash partitioning sends every row with merchant_id = 7 to the same partition, however many partitions there are (lesson 7). So the median join task fetches 43,593 records and one task fetches 346,023, eight times as many. A stage ends when its slowest task ends, so 15 cores finish early and wait. This is skew: a few keys with far more rows than the rest. In the Spark UI's stage page it shows as a maximum task duration far above the median.

Aggregations mostly survive skew. A groupBy sum adds up inside each map task before the shuffle (lesson 7's partial aggregate), so merchant 7's 300,000 payments leave the map side as four partial sums. A join has nothing to pre-combine: every payment row has to meet its merchant row in the same task.

More partitions don't help either. Merchant 7 is one key, and it lands in one partition out of 16 or out of 2,000. Nor does speculative execution, lesson 3's backup task: a copy of the hot task reads the same hot partition and is just as slow. The fixes split the key itself.

The first fix is AQE's skew join. After the map stage, AQE knows every partition's size. It calls a partition skewed when it is more than 5 times the median (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor) and also bigger than 256 MB (skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes). It splits that partition into pieces of about the advisory size, 64 MB by default, runs each piece as its own task, and gives each of those tasks a copy of the matching partition from the other side. The plan then says SortMergeJoin(skew=true). Three limits matter. The thresholds are sized for clusters: the demo's hot partition is a few megabytes, so with the defaults nothing happens. AQE cuts along map-task boundaries: each map task wrote one block of the hot partition (lesson 7), a piece is a run of whole blocks, so with 4 map tasks the hot partition becomes at most 4 pieces. That's what the demo got with the thresholds scaled down: 16 tasks became 19, and the hottest now fetches 86,635 records, a quarter of before. And Spark's docs describe skew handling for sort-merge joins only.

The second fix is salting: turn the hot key into several keys by hand. On the big side, add a salt from 0 to N-1 computed from the data, such as pmod(payment_id, 8). On the small side, copy each merchant row N times, once per salt. Join on merchant_id and the salt together. Merchant 7 is now 8 keys that hash to different tasks. In the demo the hottest task dropped to 125,793 records. That isn't an eighth of 346,023, because 8 salts hashed into 16 partitions don't land on 8 different ones: a few share a partition. You pay with N copies of the small side and a few lines of code. Never salt with rand(): when a task is retried (lesson 6), it must send every row where the first attempt sent it, or rows get lost or counted twice.

Before either, try lesson 7's fix. If the other side fits in a broadcast, a broadcast hash join never shuffles the big side, so no partition can be hot.

code.html: package sfz.batch.l08.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset import org.apache.spark.sql.Row import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.explode import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.lit import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.pmod import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.sequence import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.sum /** * A million payments, 30% of them for merchant 7, joined with 500 merchants by sort-merge join * into 16 reduce partitions. Four ways to run it, and for each one the shuffle records every join * task fetched. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() spark.conf().set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "-1") // force the sort-merge join spark.conf().set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "16") spark.conf().set("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "false") // show the skew effect alone val log = TaskLog(spark) val payments = demoPayments(spark, "skewed", hotMerchant = 7) val merchants = demoMerchants(spark) fun plain(): Dataset<Row> = payments.join(merchants, "merchant_id") fun salted(buckets: Long): Dataset<Row> = payments.withColumn("salt", pmod(col("payment_id"), lit(buckets))) .join(merchants.withColumn("salt", explode(sequence(lit(0L), lit(buckets - 1)))), arrayOf("merchant_id", "salt")) .drop("salt") val cases = listOf( Triple("AQE off", mapOf("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled" to "false"), ::plain), Triple("AQE on, default thresholds", mapOf("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled" to "true"), ::plain), Triple("AQE on, thresholds scaled down", mapOf( "spark.sql.adaptive.enabled" to "true", "spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes" to "1MB", "spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes" to "256KB"), ::plain), Triple("salted, 8 buckets, AQE off", mapOf("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled" to "false")) { salted(8) }, ) for ((label, conf, build) in cases) { conf.forEach { (k, v) -> spark.conf().set(k, v) } val df = build().groupBy("merchant_name").agg(sum("amount_cents")) val (_, stages) = log.run { df.collectAsList() } // the join stage is the one whose tasks fetched the most shuffle records val join = stages.values.maxBy { it.sum() }.sorted() val skew = planLines(df.queryExecution().executedPlan(), "SortMergeJoin").first().substringBefore(" [").replace(Regex("""^\*\(\d+\) """), "") println("%-31s %-25s %2d join tasks, records fetched: median %,6d, max %,7d (%.1fx)" .format(label, skew, join.size, join[join.size / 2], join.last(), join.last().toDouble() / join[join.size / 2])) } spark.stop() }

AQE off                         SortMergeJoin             16 join tasks, records fetched: median 43,593, max 346,023 (7.9x)
AQE on, default thresholds      SortMergeJoin             16 join tasks, records fetched: median 43,593, max 346,023 (7.9x)
AQE on, thresholds scaled down  SortMergeJoin(skew=true)  19 join tasks, records fetched: median 43,619, max  86,635 (2.0x)
salted, 8 buckets, AQE off      SortMergeJoin             16 join tasks, records fetched: median 45,760, max 125,793 (2.7x)

With AQE off, the hot task fetched 7.9 times the median: merchant 7's 300,000 payments plus its partition's share of the rest. AQE with its default thresholds changed nothing, because the hot partition is a few megabytes and the threshold is 256 MB. With the thresholds scaled down, the plan says SortMergeJoin(skew=true): AQE cut the hot partition into 4 pieces, one per map task (the payments are 4 files), so 16 tasks became 19 and the worst one fetched 86,635 records. Salting needs no AQE at all and brought the worst task to 125,793. The record counts come out the same on every machine, because the data is generated the same way every run.

sections.h: cache() keeps a result in executor memory, at a price
sections.html:
Lesson 6 ended with a cost of laziness: every action runs its plan from the files again. The nightly job builds one intermediate result, totals per card, and runs two reports on it. Two actions, so two scans and two shuffles.

Version 1: write the intermediate result to Parquet and read it back. It works, it survives a crash, and it costs a full write plus a folder someone must clean up.

Version 2: cache(). Calling it marks the DataFrame and does nothing else. The first action that computes the DataFrame also keeps each partition in the memory of the executor that computed it, as compressed column batches of 10,000 rows. From then on Spark's cache manager looks for that plan inside every new query, and a query whose plan contains it reads the stored batches instead: the plan shows InMemoryTableScan. The match is by plan, so even a fresh spark.read() of the same files finds the cache. For a DataFrame, cache() means persist(MEMORY_AND_DISK): partitions that don't fit in memory go to the executor's local disk.

The Try it measures two shared results, each read by two reports. For totals per card, a groupBy over a million cards, the two reports took 11.0 seconds without a cache and 1.7 seconds from it: the cache saved both reports from repeating the scan and the shuffle. For the captured payments, a filtered Parquet scan, the cache barely helped: 2.7 seconds without it, 2.3 seconds with it, and filling it took 8.4 seconds, longer than both reports together. (These times come from a laptop that was very busy with other work; yours will be shorter, and the ratios are what to compare.)

So a cache has a price list:

  • The first action pays extra, to encode and store every row. Cache something that's used once and you pay for nothing.
  • A cheap source doesn't need it. Parquet with pushdown and column pruning (lesson 5) is already a fast way to re-read data.
  • Cached blocks share the executor's memory with execution: sort buffers, hash tables, shuffle buffers. A big cache leaves less room for the next join, which then spills to disk; when execution needs the room, Spark evicts cached blocks, and they're recomputed or read back from disk.
  • The cache lives until unpersist() or the end of the application. A long-running service that caches per request fills its executors.

Cache a result when two or more actions reuse it, when it's expensive to rebuild (a shuffle, a join, a heavy expression), and when it fits. Cache it after the filter and the select, so memory holds only what the reuse needs, and call unpersist() in a finally once the last action is done.

try.title: Cache a cheap result and an expensive one
steps: Run CacheDemo. For two shared results, it times two reports without a cache, the action that fills the cache, and the same two reports from the cache.
Before reading: which of the two results will gain from the cache, and which might not?
Compare the bytes in memory with the size of the Parquet files. Which is bigger, and why?

code.title: CacheDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l08.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset import org.apache.spark.sql.Row import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.count import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.sum import java.io.File /** * When cache() pays and when it doesn't. Two reports run over a shared intermediate result, with and * without a cache: first a cheap one (a filtered Parquet scan), then an expensive one (totals per * card: a shuffle of a million rows). */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() val path = File("build/l07/payments").absolutePath demoPayments(spark) fun ms(block: () -> Unit): Double { val t0 = System.nanoTime(); block(); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6 } fun best(block: () -> Unit) = (1..3).minOf { ms(block) } // the shared result is rebuilt by a function, so each call is a new DataFrame with the same plan fun compare(label: String, shared: () -> Dataset<Row>, reports: (Dataset<Row>) -> Unit) { reports(shared()) // warm-up val plain = best { reports(shared()) } val cached = shared().cache() val fill = ms { cached.count() } // the first action fills the cache val fromCache = best { reports(shared()) } // same plan: the cache manager swaps it in val plan = planLines(shared().groupBy().count().queryExecution().executedPlan(), "InMemoryTableScan").firstOrNull() ?: "(no cache in plan)" val info = spark.sparkContext().getRDDStorageInfo().single() println(label) println(" two reports without cache: %6.0f ms".format(plain)) println(" filling the cache: %6.0f ms (%,d bytes in memory, %d partitions)".format(fill, info.memSize(), info.numCachedPartitions())) println(" two reports from the cache:%6.0f ms plan reads: %s".format(fromCache, plan)) cached.unpersist(true) } compare("cheap: captured payments, a filtered Parquet scan (%,d bytes of files)".format( File(path).listFiles { f -> f.name.endsWith(".parquet") }!!.sumOf { it.length() }), { spark.read().parquet(path).where(col("status").equalTo("CAPTURED")) }, ) { df -> df.groupBy("merchant_id").agg(sum("amount_cents")).collectAsList() df.groupBy("card_country").count().collectAsList() } compare("expensive: totals per card, a groupBy over a million cards", { spark.read().parquet(path).groupBy("card_id").agg(sum("amount_cents").alias("total"), count("*").alias("n")) }, ) { df -> df.where(col("n").gt(2)).count() df.orderBy(col("total").desc()).limit(5).collectAsList() } spark.stop() }

  filling the cache:           8402 ms  (4,342,856 bytes in memory, 4 partitions)
  two reports from the cache:  2333 ms  plan reads: InMemoryTableScan

The expensive result gained more than six times on the two reports; the cheap one gained little and cost more to fill than it saved. Filling a cache is a full computation plus the work of encoding every row into column batches, so a result read only once never pays it back. The cached captured payments take 4.3 MB of memory for 250,288 rows and six columns, compressed, while the Parquet files hold all million rows in 14.5 MB: Parquet's encodings (lesson 5) are tighter than the cache's. Both plans read InMemoryTableScan once the cache is filled. Times depend heavily on your machine and on what else it's doing.

refs.title: RDD persistence and storage levels (RDD programming guide)

analogy: Catalyst is a route planner working from a paper map before the trip: it knows the roads and their lengths, and it picks the shortest route on paper, cutting out detours you wrote by habit. AQE is the satnav that checks live traffic at each junction and re-routes when a road it assumed was busy turns out empty. Skew is a single toll booth that every lorry from one depot must use while the other booths stand idle; opening more booths doesn't help unless you send that depot's lorries to several of them. A cache is parking a loaded van at the warehouse door because you'll need its contents twice tonight. The analogy breaks at the junctions: a satnav can re-route mid-road, but AQE can only change the plan at a stage boundary, after a shuffle has finished. A stage that's already running runs to the end with the plan it started with.
world: You've met all four ideas outside Spark. Oracle's optimizer rewrites your SQL with transformations much like Catalyst's rules, and since 12c it has adaptive plans that can switch a nested-loops join to a hash join during the first run, once a statistics collector has counted the real rows; that's AQE's broadcast switch in another engine. Skew is the Kafka topic keyed by merchant_id where one marketplace merchant makes partition 3 lag by minutes while the other consumers idle; the fixes match too: change the key, or add a suffix (a salt) to the hot key and give up per-key ordering for it. And cache() is the Caffeine cache in a Quarkus service, with the same questions you already ask there: is the value reused enough to be worth the memory, and who evicts it when you're done?
mistake: The common mistake is treating cache() as a free speed-up and adding it everywhere, usually right after spark.read(). Three things go wrong. A DataFrame used once pays the cost of encoding and storing every row and gets nothing back. A DataFrame cached before its filter holds every row and every column of the table, crowding out the memory that joins and sorts need, so they spill to disk. And nobody calls unpersist(), so in a long-running application the cached blocks pile up until the executors run short of memory. People do it because notebooks reward it: the second cell runs faster. The fix is to cache on purpose: only a result that two or more actions reuse, only after the filter and the select, and with unpersist() in a finally block once the last action is done. Check the plan for InMemoryTableScan to see that the reuse really happens.

worked.title: Fix a settlement join that stalls on one task

steps.say: The nightly job joins the day's payments with merchants and has started taking 40 minutes instead of 6. In the Spark UI, the join stage has 400 tasks; 399 finish in under 30 seconds and one runs for 35 minutes. One slow task in an otherwise fast stage is skew until proven otherwise. Find the key.
steps.code: // 1. which keys have the most rows? (run on a sample or one day) payments.groupBy("merchant_id").count() .orderBy(col("count").desc()).show(5) // merchant_id count // 7 61,204,880 <- a marketplace: 31% of the day // 311 412,903 // 88 398,117

steps.say: First question: can the other side be broadcast? A broadcast hash join doesn't shuffle the payments, so there is no hot partition at all. Here it can't: the join is with a 6 GB merchant-risk table, far too big to copy to every executor.
steps.code: // 2. check the small side's real size before anything clever merchantRisk.count() // 92 million rows, about 6 GB: no broadcast

steps.say: Second: is AQE allowed to split the hot partition? It's on by default, but a partition must be over 5 times the median and over 256 MB. The hot partition is 18 GB, so it qualifies; check the plan for the skew marker after a run. If it's there, AQE split it along the map tasks' outputs.

If AQE can't help (a join type it doesn't handle, a skewed side with few map tasks, or a partition just under the threshold), salt the hot key by hand. Salt only merchant 7, so the risk table grows by 15 rows, not 15 times.
steps.code: // 4. salt one key into 16 sub-keys val hot = col("merchant_id").equalTo(7) val p = payments.withColumn("salt", `when`(hot, pmod(col("payment_id"), lit(16L))).otherwise(lit(0L))) val r = merchantRisk.withColumn("salt", explode(`when`(hot, sequence(lit(0L), lit(15L))).otherwise(array(lit(0L))))) val joined = p.join(r, arrayOf("merchant_id", "salt")).drop("salt")

lab.title: Read the optimizer, split a hot key, cache on purpose
steps: Run the tests. They fail: two of the three files throw TODO, and NightlyReports runs but caches the wrong thing.

Write PlanReader.filtersBelowJoins: walk the optimized logical plan from the root and, once you've passed a Join, collect every Filter condition as SQL. The test writes the filter above the join and expects your walk to find both halves of it below. Then rulesThatFired, from the planning tracker.

Write SkewedJoin.salted. The test data gives merchant 7 30% of 40,000 payments, joined into 16 partitions with AQE off. The plain join's hottest task reads 13,938 records; yours must read less than half of that and return exactly the same rows.

Four settings do it: spark.sql.adaptive.enabled, spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled, spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes well below 500 KB (100KB works) and spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes below that (64KB).

drill.title: Salt a join from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the Kotlin that joins payments with merchants on merchant_id with every key salted into 8 sub-keys. Then write the two lines you'd check afterwards to prove it changed nothing about the result.

answer.html: val n = 8L val p = payments.withColumn("salt", pmod(col("payment_id"), lit(n))) // from data: a retry gets the same salt val m = merchants.withColumn("salt", explode(sequence(lit(0L), lit(n - 1)))) // every merchant once per salt val joined = p.join(m, arrayOf("merchant_id", "salt")).drop("salt") // same rows as before, no more and no fewer check(joined.count() == payments.join(merchants, "merchant_id").count()) check(joined.columns().toSet() == payments.join(merchants, "merchant_id").columns().toSet())

recap: Catalyst holds a query as a tree and rewrites it with rules until nothing changes: filters move below joins, unused columns go, constants fold. explain("extended") shows the parsed, analyzed, optimized and physical plans.
The physical plan is chosen from size estimates, and after a filter the estimate is usually the whole input.
AQE runs the plan stage by stage and re-plans at each shuffle with real sizes: it merges small partitions, switches to a broadcast join, and splits skewed partitions.
Skew is one key with far more rows than the rest; one task does its work while the others wait. Broadcast if you can, let AQE split it (over 5x the median and 256 MB), or salt the key by hand.
cache() stores a result in executor memory on its first action and swaps InMemoryTableScan into later plans. It pays only when reused; cache after the filter and unpersist() when done.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "AQE is on by default, so I don't need to think about join strategies or skew any more." Explain what AQE can and can't do, using what happens at a stage boundary.
explain.answer: AQE only acts at stage boundaries. Spark runs the plan one query stage at a time, and when a stage that ends in a shuffle finishes, the driver knows the real bytes in every shuffle partition. AQE then re-plans the rest with those sizes: it merges tiny partitions, switches a sort-merge join to a broadcast when one side turned out small, and splits a partition that is both over 5 times the median and over 256 MB. So it fixes bad estimates, but late. A broadcast it switches to still paid for the big side's shuffle write, because that map stage had already run; planning the broadcast up front with a hint avoids it. Its skew handling only covers sort-merge joins, only past the thresholds, and only along map-task boundaries, so a hot key in a 40 MB partition or a key it can't split stays slow, and salting is still your tool. And it can't change anything inside a stage that's already running. AQE removes a lot of tuning, but you still read the final plan to see what it did.

deeper.html:
Catalyst's estimates can be better than file sizes. ANALYZE TABLE payments COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS merchant_id, amount_cents stores row counts, distinct counts, min, max and null counts in the catalog, and with spark.sql.cbo.enabled=true the cost-based optimizer uses them to estimate how many rows a filter keeps and to reorder joins (spark.sql.cbo.joinReorder.enabled). Few pipelines keep those statistics fresh, which is why AQE's measured sizes matter more in practice. Table formats help here: an Iceberg table (lesson 11) keeps row counts and column bounds for every file in its metadata.

Two runtime tricks sit between Catalyst and AQE. Dynamic partition pruning: when a partitioned fact table is joined with a filtered dimension, Spark runs the dimension side first and uses its keys to skip partitions of the fact table at scan time (spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled, on by default); the plan shows it as dynamicpruningexpression. Runtime filters do something similar for columns that aren't partition columns, by sending a Bloom filter of the join keys to the other side's scan.

cache() has two relatives. persist(StorageLevel) picks where blocks live (memory only, disk only, serialized, replicated). checkpoint() writes the result to reliable storage and cuts the lineage, so a failure later never recomputes the expensive part; it costs a full write, like writing Parquet yourself. And Spark 4.3 added opt-in single-task execution for small queries (spark.sql.optimizer.singleTaskExecution.enabled), which skips shuffles entirely when the data is tiny: the optimizer deciding not to be distributed at all.
